definition: The Hittite capital, near modern Bogazkoy in central Turkey. Its archives held tens of thousands of cuneiform tablets, including the myths of Kumarbi, Ullikummi, Telipinu, Illuyanka and Appu.
The wedge-shaped writing system used across the ancient Near East, impressed into clay with a cut reed. Hittite scribes wrote their myths in cuneiform, often borrowing Sumerian and Akkadian signs.

A language and culture of northern Syria and southeastern Anatolia, attested from the third millennium BCE. Hurrian myths of Kumarbi and Teshub reached the Hittites through Kizzuwatna and were translated into Hittite.

A group of Hurrian songs about kingship among the gods, known from Hittite copies at Hattusa. It includes the Song of Kumarbi, the Song of Hedammu and the Song of Ullikummi, and tells of Kumarbi's repeated attempts to overthrow Teshub.
A Hittite spring and New Year festival, celebrated at Hattusa and Nerik, when the land was meant to blossom and enjoy peace. The myth of Teshub and Illuyanka was recited as part of it.
The Hurrian storm god, king of the gods and opponent of Kumarbi. The Hittites identified him with their own storm god Tarhunna; his city was Kummiya, his wife Hebat, and his brother Tasmisu.
A Hittite vegetation god, son of the storm god, whose anger and disappearance cause drought, hunger and sterility. His myth was recited with a ritual to restore fertility to the land and the king.
A Hittite mother goddess whose name means 'grandmother'. She appears in the Telipinu myth, sending a bee to find the vanished god and bring him home.
A giant of diorite made by Kumarbi to destroy the storm god Teshub. Hidden on the shoulder of Ubelluri, he grows to the sky and is cut down only with Ea's ancient copper tool.
An Indo-European people who ruled central Anatolia from Hattusa between about 1650 and 1180 BCE. Their archives preserve both native Anatolian myths and Hurrian stories translated into Hittite.
